opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to where the information actually originates. A foundation model is essentially a compressed representation of the world, and that knowledge has to come from somewhere real: human writing, code, images, physical measurements, the long tail of things people have actually done and said. Synthetic data, almost by definition, is generated by some existing process, whether that's a model, a simulator, or a set of rules someone wrote down. So it can only contain information that was already present in that generator, plus whatever structure you impose on it.

When you already have a strong base model, synthetic data is incredibly useful because it lets you reshape, amplify, and focus what the model already sort of knows. You can generate reasoning traces, cover edge cases, balance distributions, create verifiable math or coding problems where you can check the answer automatically. That's enhancement: you're improving the signal-to-noise ratio and steering the model toward capabilities that are latent but underdeveloped.

But if you try to build from scratch purely on synthetic data, you hit a kind of closed loop. The model learns the generator's view of the world, including its blind spots and biases, and those errors compound. People have seen this as model collapse, where the distribution narrows over generations and you lose the tails, which is often where the interesting, rare knowledge lives.

Coming from a simulation and graphics background, I see a nice analogy there. A physics simulator can produce endless training data, and it's great for robotics or for learning specific dynamics. But the simulator only knows the physics you programmed into it. If your friction model is wrong, everything trained on it inherits that error. That's the sim-to-real gap. You still need real-world data to anchor things.

So my view is that real data provides the grounding and the diversity, and synthetic data provides the leverage. You need the first to have something worth amplifying with the second.

r001.rationale: It says synthetic data may come from “a set of rules someone wrote down,” attributing those rules to human authorship.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic data can contain only what is present in its generator and that a simulator knows only the physics programmed into it, describing limited coverage of the real world.

r003.rationale: It notes that a programmed friction model can be wrong and that training inherits the error, indicating simulated rules can diverge from actual physical laws.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think it gets at something fundamental about where information actually comes from.

When you generate synthetic data, you're always generating it from some model of the world. That could be a physics simulator, a rendering engine, or another neural network. But whatever that generator is, it already encodes a set of assumptions about how the world works. The synthetic data can only ever be as rich as the generator behind it. So if you try to build a foundation model purely from synthetic data, you're essentially training a model to learn the biases and simplifications of your generator, not the real world. You end up with a closed loop. Information doesn't come from nowhere.

Real data is different because it's sampled from the actual distribution, with all its messiness, long tails, and the things nobody thought to simulate. That's where the "foundation" in foundation model comes from. The model's broad understanding of the world has to be grounded in observations of the world.

Where synthetic data really shines is in filling gaps. Once you have a model that already understands the world reasonably well from real data, you can use simulation to cover the cases that are rare, dangerous, or expensive to collect. In robotics, for example, you can't crash a thousand robots to learn what failure looks like, but you can simulate it. You can vary lighting, materials, object poses, and generate thousands of variations around a real scenario. That targeted augmentation makes the model more robust and more sample-efficient.

So I'd frame it this way: real data provides the prior, and synthetic data sharpens the posterior. The simulator is a tool for interpolating and extrapolating around what you've already observed, but it can't replace observation itself. If you flip that order and try to bootstrap from simulation alone, you're building on sand.

r001.rationale: The response says generators encode assumptions, but does not attribute those assumptions or generation rules to human design.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic data inherits a generator’s limits and contrasts this with real-world messiness, long tails, and situations nobody thought to simulate.

r003.rationale: The response mentions generator biases and simplifications, but does not clearly state that synthetic generation rules can diverge from actual physical laws.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between creating information and making better use of information you already have. If you use an existing model to generate synthetic data, that data largely reflects what the model already knows, including its biases and blind spots. It can make that knowledge easier to learn, but it doesn’t automatically give you new grounding in the real world.

That’s why synthetic data can be very useful for enhancing a foundation model. You can generate examples for a particular task, explore variations, and filter the results using something reliable, like a compiler or a simulator. That can provide a much stronger learning signal.

But if you start entirely from model-generated data, where does the original knowledge come from? You need some source of information outside that loop. I wouldn’t say synthetic data can never build a model from scratch—if it comes from a simulator, for example, the simulator contributes knowledge. But for a broad foundation model, synthetic data alone doesn’t replace the diversity and grounding of real-world observations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data generated by existing models or simulators, but does not attribute generation rules to human design.

r002.rationale: It notes that synthetic data may inherit a model’s blind spots and lacks real-world diversity, but does not state that its generation rules cover only a limited subset of real-world situations.

r003.rationale: The response says a simulator can contribute knowledge, but does not say synthetic generation rules may diverge from physical laws.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is that synthetic data can reorganize and amplify knowledge, but it needs a source of knowledge to begin with. If you use an existing model to generate training data, that data inherits both the capabilities and the limitations of that model. You can make certain skills easier to learn, but you don’t automatically introduce new information about the world.

That’s why synthetic data can be very useful for improving a foundation model. You already have a broad base of knowledge, and you can generate more examples for a particular task, filter them, and train on the good ones.

But I wouldn’t say building from scratch is fundamentally impossible. If the synthetic data comes from a simulator or another system that provides independent feedback, then you have a source of information beyond the model itself. The important question is where that grounding comes from. Simply having a model generate more text doesn’t replace it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models, simulators, and sources of information, but does not say humans design the rules used to generate synthetic data.

r002.rationale: It says model-generated data inherits the model’s limitations, but does not state that generation rules cover only a limited subset of real-world situations.

r003.rationale: It mentions grounding from simulators or other systems, but does not say synthetic data generation rules may diverge from physical laws.
